newsitem.title: UK: UK mergers hit record level in first half of 1997.
newsitem.headline: UK mergers hit record level in first half of 1997.

text.p: British mergers and acquisitions activity reached record levels in the first half of 1997, according to figures released by magazine Acquisitions Monthly on Monday.
"Public bids announced in the first half of 1997 were at their highest value ever, at 22.3 billion pounds ($38 billion). The previous record of 21 billion was set in the first half of 1989," it said.

The magazine's editor Philip Healey said several more billion-pound deals were promised for the second half of the year, adding the investment banks' optimism was borne out by the recent merger between British health and technology group Amersham International Plc and Norway's Nycomed.

Healey said bankers, brokers, accountants, lawyers and public relations consultants had together earned an estimated 600 million pounds during the half-year period. If fees continued at this rate, 1997 could be a more lucrative year for the advisors than 1996's record of 1.1 billion pounds, he added.

British investment banking group Schroders topped the mergers and acquisitions advisory league table, with a total of 17 public and private deals worth a total of 5.81 billion pounds. For 1996 as a whole Schroders came fourth in the rankings.
Baring Brothers, the corporate finance wing of Dutch-owned ING Barings which clinched the number one position for 1995 and 1996, was second.
It advised on deals worth a total of 5.58 billion pounds. Most of this was in the form of private deals worth 4.28 billion pounds.
Schroders advised on public deals worth 4.64 billion with the remainder made up of private deals.
Its list of public deals included advising East Midlands Electricity on its takeover by Dominion Resources Inc and London Electricity on its purchase by Entergy Corp.
Acquisitions Monthly highlighted a strong performance by UBS which ranked third, compared with its fifth place in the first half of 1996.
It also pointed out that non-British banks did well, with U.S. firms -- led by Goldman Sachs at number seven -- accounting for six of the top 20.

N M Rothschild, another British bank that has managed to retain its independence also made a strong showing, with seven deals taking it to fourth place, against its fifth position for 1996 as a whole.

At the bottom of the table, Dresdner Kleinwort Benson, which ranked third for the period a year ago, only managed to make 19th position. And NatWest Markets, which was 12th for 1996 as a whole, was 20th.
